readerTitle: Revenue fell 20%. Where did it go?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (동네 피자집 + 온라인 주문 페이지) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 매출 하락은 해결책부터 찾는 문제가 아니라, 문제를 정의하고 쪼갠 뒤 가장 큰 조각부터 원인을 좁혀 가는 문제다.
misconception: 매출이 떨어지면 일단 할인이나 광고로 손님을 더 불러오는 것이 먼저다.

sources.text: 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시
문제 정의, 문제 분해, 가설 사고, 80/20, 다섯 번의 왜 (THK-07 유닛 개념)

factChecks.note: 작년 같은 달과 비교해 계절 요인을 배제한다는 설정은 가상입니다. 실제로는 여러 해 데이터를 함께 봐야 한다는 점을 Watch out 카드에 적었습니다.

cards.title: Revenue fell 20%. Where did it go?
body: Rosa runs a busy neighborhood pizzeria. Last month brought in $48,000. The same month last year brought in $60,000.
Her first instinct is to print 2-for-1 coupons. You're going to help her find out why first, one decision at a time.

image.label: Pizzeria owner staring at a sales report
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 동네 피자집 카운터. 주인이 영수증 뭉치와 노트북을 보며 고민하는 모습. 화면에 아래로 꺾인 매출 그래프. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What's your first move?
body: Rosa wants to act this week. Staff have opinions. The numbers sit in her point-of-sale system.

options.text: Run the 2-for-1 promotion now to win customers back
options.feedback: It feels decisive, but it treats a cause no one has found yet. If the problem is elsewhere, Rosa gives away margin and still loses revenue.

options.text: Pin down exactly what fell, since when, and compared with what
options.feedback: A few minutes of definition tells you whether this is a season, a sudden break or a slow slide. Each one points to a different fix.

options.text: Ask the staff why they think sales dropped
options.feedback: Staff see things the numbers miss, so it's worth doing. But without a clear problem, you'll collect guesses, not leads.

cards.title: A vague worry becomes a clear problem.
body: Rosa compares the same month last year, so the season is roughly equal. She checks weekly sales and sees the drop started suddenly in week two, not slowly.
Her problem statement: **Since week two, revenue is running about 20% below the same weeks last year.** A sudden start suggests something changed. That's already more useful than "sales are bad."

cards.title: How do you split the $12,000 gap?
body: Revenue comes from three places: dine-in, phone pickup orders and online orders. You can only dig into one split first.

options.text: By channel: dine-in, phone and online
options.feedback: The parts add up to the total, and each channel has different customers and different ways to break. One split can rule out two-thirds of the business.
Useful if one dish fell out of favor. But a sudden, broad drop rarely comes from a single pizza.
It can reveal a staffing or opening-hours issue. Here it would show every day down a bit, which doesn't narrow much.

cards.title: One channel holds almost the whole drop.
body: Phone orders didn't move. Dine-in slipped $1,200. Online fell $10,800, which is **90% of the gap**. Average online order is still $30. There are just fewer orders: 240 instead of 600.

cards.title: Which hypothesis do you test first?
body: Online orders dropped 60%, suddenly, starting in week two. Everything else barely moved.

options.text: A new pizza place opened nearby
options.feedback: Possible, but a rival would usually pull dine-in and phone customers too. Worth checking second.

options.text: Something broke in the online ordering path
options.feedback: A sudden drop in one channel fits a break. It's also cheap to test: place an order yourself on a phone tonight.

options.text: Customers are bored with the menu
options.feedback: Boredom builds slowly and hits every channel. Chasing it means a costly menu redesign aimed at the wrong cause.

cards.title: Rosa orders a pizza from her own website.
body: Why fewer orders? People still visit the order page, but few finish. Why? On phones, the *Pay* button now sits below the screen and won't scroll into view. Why? A designer added new menu photos in week two. Why wasn't it caught? He only tested on a laptop. Why? No one checks the order flow after a site change.
The button is fixed in a day. The real fix is the last why: **a phone test order after every change.**

image.label: Phone screen with the pay button cut off
image.brief: 스마트폰 화면에 피자 주문 페이지. 큰 음식 사진들이 화면을 채우고, 'Pay' 버튼이 화면 아래로 반쯤 잘려 보임. 옆에 노트북 화면에서는 같은 버튼이 정상으로 보이는 대비. 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The button works again. Now what?
body: Two days after the fix, online orders are picking up.

options.text: Call it solved and move on
options.feedback: You save time now, but you haven't confirmed the fix closes the gap. The $1,200 dine-in dip is still unexplained.

options.text: Track weekly online orders for a month and add the phone test to every site change
options.feedback: You confirm the cause by watching the number recover, and the checklist stops the same break from coming back.

options.text: Hire an agency to rebuild the whole website
options.feedback: It feels thorough, but it's expensive and adds new chances for things to break. The cause was one untested change.

cards.title: Real drops are rarely this tidy.
body: Here one cause explained 90% of the gap. Often two or three causes overlap, and fixing the biggest leaves a smaller one hiding underneath.

A split also only helps if the parts add up to the total. And one year of comparison can mislead. A rainy month or a local event can look like a trend. Treat each answer as a lead to confirm, not a verdict.

cards.title: Find where the money went before you try to win it back.
body: Your four decisions used four ideas from this unit:
list: **Define the problem:** what fell, since when, compared with what
**Break it into parts:** split the total into channels that add up
**Hypothesis and 80/20:** test the likeliest cause in the biggest piece first
**Ask why five times:** keep going until you reach a fix that prevents a repeat
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your last revenue number and split it into three or four parts that add up. Which part moved most?
